[14] The psychotherapy report in item (a) is dated August 13, 2020. The report indicates that the Principal Appellant "is exhibiting symptoms consistent with post-traumatic stress, generalized anxiety, and major depression."8 Counsel argues that the Appellant was only aware of her psychological difficulties after the RPD rejection. On this basis, I find the report is admissible under 110(4). It is credible for the purposes of admission as it is issued by a psychotherapist. Counsel argues that "[t]he Psych report shows that the Appellant was pregnant during the hearing."9 I disagree. The psychotherapy report does not mention any pregnancy during the hearing. It states that the Principal Appellant was pregnant when she entered Canada.10 The report provides information that was not before the RPD and it is relevant to an assessment of the Principal Appellant's credibility. I admit item (a) into evidence. I find that it does not require a hearing under 110(6) as it does not justify allowing or rejecting the claim.11

[15] The affidavit in item (b) was purportedly sworn by the Principal Appellant's mother on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020. It includes an allegation that in XXXX 2020, her home was visited by the Appellants' persecutors demanding to know their location and threatening that the next visit will be deadly.12 I find that the evidence post-dates the RPD's negative determination and therefore meets the requirements of subsection 110(4). However, I do not find the evidence to be credible having regard to the source and circumstances in which it came into existence.

[16] Counsel argues that the new evidence is credible because it is a "sworn statement of facts" before a Nigerian Notary Public.13 However, the Principal Appellant's mother has not signed above the line 'deponent.'14 This despite the fact that the document bears the stamp, seal and signature of a notary public indicating that the document was sworn on XXXX XXXX, 2020.15 Nothing in evidence or in Counsel's submissions comments on this irregularity.

[17] There is a rebuttable presumption that documents issued by foreign authorities are genuine.16 However, I find that there are irregularities on the face of the evidence which undermines its credibility and reliability and rebuts this presumption. The objective evidence states that "an affidavit will carry 'the signature of the deponent, the signature of the Commissioner for Oaths/Notary that swore the document, and the seal/stamp of the court/Notary.'"17 The Nigerian Evidence Act at section 117(4) requires that "an affidavit when sworn shall be signed by the deponent or if he cannot write or is blind, marked by him personally with his mark."18 Where the declarant was prevented from placing a signature on the statement, the Nigerian Evidence Act at section 119(3) requires a 'mark' be applied and that "the jurat shall state that fact, and that the mark was made in the presence of the person before whom it was taken."19 No such reference is made in the jurat of the declaration before me.20

[18] I acknowledge that superficial errors should not be unreasonably focused on in assessing a document's credibility as "clerical errors are possible even in countries where public administration have access to vast resources."21 However, I do not find these irregularities to be mere clerical errors. The signature, stamp and seal of a notary public are security features added to a sworn statement. They confirm that the deponent or affiant has appeared before the commissioner or notary and has sworn or affirmed as to the contents of the statement. It is only after this happens that a document is signed, stamped, and sealed by the notary or commissioner. It simply is not credible that a notary public would stamp and sign an affidavit without it first being signed by the deponent. The Federal Court found in Morka that the RPD's rejection of an unsigned affidavit was reasonable, noting that such an anomaly is apparent on its face.22 I find that these irregularities undermine the credibility of the source and circumstances in which the affidavit came into existence. The RAD is entitled to assess a document's irregularities in evaluating its credibility under the Singh factors.23

[19] I have also taken into consideration the stamps and seal present on the document. However, I do not find that this resolves the credibility concerns as it does not explain why the Principal Appellant's mother did not sign the affidavit or why a notary public signed the document in the absence of the signature of deponent.

[20] I also have concerns with the content of the statement. The Principal Appellant's mother alleges that she is Christian and the Principal Appellant "grew up in a Christian home."24 This differs from the Principal Appellant's own inconsistent evidence about her religious upbringing, including that she comes from a Muslim family and converted to Christianity against her parents' wishes.25 Nothing in evidence or submissions comments on the inconsistency as between the Principal Appellant's evidence and her mother's statement.

[21] As I have credibility concerns regarding the source and circumstances in which the evidence in item (b) came into existence, I do not find it credible. I therefore find it inadmissible.
The evidence in item (b) is inadmissible and cannot trigger a hearing under 110(6)

[30] In Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board, the Supreme Court of Canada set out the test to determine the existence of a reasonable apprehension of bias:
[The] test is "what would an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically - and having thought the matter through - conclude. Would he think that it is more likely than not that [the decision-maker], whether consciously or unconsciously, would not decide fairly."36

[31] The grounds for the apprehension of bias must be substantial, and a high burden rests on the Appellant who seeks to establish either an actual bias or an apprehension of bias.37 A real likelihood of bias must be demonstrated.38 An allegation cannot rest on "mere suspicion, pure conjecture or mere impressions" and it "must be supported by material evidence."39 Counsel has failed to provide any examples which would support a finding that a reasonable person would conclude that the RPD would not decide fairly. Counsel merely disagrees with the RPD's findings. I find that an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically, would not think it more likely than not that the RPD would not decide fairly. Having independently assessed the entire Record, including the audio-recording, I find that the RPD did not display a reasonable apprehension of bias. As discussed below, the RPD was correct to draw negative credibility inferences based on significant inconsistencies in the evidence.
The RPD's overall credibility assessment is correct
Testimony about two demands for son's facial incision is not inconsistent

[32] The RPD found that the Principal Appellant provided inconsistent evidence about when she learned about the incision rites and that she omitted a family meeting from the BOC. Having independently assessed the evidence, I find no inconsistency or omission arises. In her BOC, the Principal Appellant describes learning about the facial incisions after the birth of her son and she also describes an incident after her son turned one year old where she was informed that the incision rites would soon be completed. This is consistent with her testimony.40 In addition, while she did not explicitly identify the incident after her son turned one year old as a "family meeting", she was clear in her BOC that she was "informed by the family."41 I find that the RPD erred and I do not rely on this RPD finding in my independent assessment.

[33] In her BOC, the Principal Appellant provided inconsistent accounts of her religion. She states that she is a "Converted Muslim (born Christian)" and also that she comes "from a [M]uslim family but converted to Christianity while I was in secondary school, although my parents were not happy they accepted it."42 She testified that she is Christian and converted to Christianity in high school.43 She also testified that her father is Muslim and her Mother is Christian.44 When asked to explain the inconsistency in evidence, she explained that she made a mistake, she was pregnant when she came Canada, and she meant to be consistent in her BOC that she converted to Christianity.45 The RPD did not accept this explanation, finding it reasonable for her to be consistent about her religion and religious conversion throughout her BOC and testimony.46 The RPD further found that this is material to the claim as she alleged that her in-laws wanted to force her to convert to Islam and accept the family traditions.47 I agree.

[40] Counsel argues that the RPD failed to consider the Principal Appellant's explanation for the trip to Saudi Arabia.60 I disagree. The RPD's concern was not with her decision to take this trip, but rather with the omission of the trip from the BOC and her allegation that she was in hiding in Nigeria when she was in fact travelling in Saudi Arabia. The trip to Saudi Arabia in XXXX 2015 undermines her alleged time in hiding in Nigeria.

[41] The Principal Appellant completed her BOC in English and filed an amendment where she failed to correct her allegation that she was hiding in Nigeria during this trip abroad.61 I do not find that her failure to recall this event is explained by her pregnancy or psychological symptoms. The Saudi Arabia trip is not connected to a short-term memory or a traumatic event. I appreciate that pregnancy can cause forgetfulness and that the Principal Appellant has trouble with short term-recall and her concentration difficulties interfere with her fluidity of thought. However, I do not find that these difficulties would reasonably cause her to state that she was in hiding in Nigeria when she was in fact travelling abroad, in Saudi Arabia. Whether the Principal Appellant was in hiding in Nigeria in XXXX 2015, as alleged, is material to her claim. This is not a peripheral detail. Her Saudi Arabia trip undermines her allegation that she was living in hiding from her persecutors in Nigeria during this period.

[42] I agree with the RPD that it is reasonable to expect the Principal Appellant to include her trip to Saudi Arabia in her BOC and provide consistent evidence about whether she was hiding in Nigeria or travelling abroad. The RPD correctly drew a negative inference. In my independent assessment, I find the BOC omission and inconsistency undermine the Appellants' credibility.
Material omission of trip to XXXX from the BOC

[43] The Principal Appellant also failed to disclose a further trip in her BOC, this time to XXXX in XXXX 2014 with the in-laws that she fears. The Principal Appellant explained that "we were in XXXX before those, they started threatening me" and that before this trip there was "nothing serious about it."62 However, this conflicts with her BOC where she alleges that the threats began shortly after her son's birth in XXXX 2013, when the "harassment increased" and she was "severally [sic] mistreated by my mother-in-law."63 The Principal Appellant also explained that she omitted the XXXX trip because she was pregnant and forgetful when she wrote her BOC.64 The RPD found that the omission was not reasonably explained.65 I agree.

[44] Counsel raises one error with respect to this RPD finding - that the RPD improperly drew a negative inference from the fact that the in-laws never tried to harm the Minor Appellant on this trip.66 In my view, Counsel has misapprehended the RPD's finding. The RPD did not draw an adverse inference because the persecutors did not harm the Minor Appellant. While the RPD expressed "surprise" that the Minor Appellant was not harmed on this trip, it drew an adverse inference based on the omission of this trip from the BOC.67 In my independent assessment, I draw no adverse inference based on the absence of harm on this trip. I agree with the RPD that the trip to XXXX is material to the claim. It was taken with the agents of persecution after the Principal Appellant alleges in her BOC that the harm, harassment, and mistreatment increased.

[45] In my independent assessment, I have considered whether the Principal Appellant's pregnancy and psychological evidence reasonably explain the BOC omission. I appreciate that pregnancy can cause forgetfulness and that the Principal Appellant has trouble with short term-recall and her concentration difficulties interfere with her fluidity of thought. However, the XXXX trip is not connected to a short-term memory or a traumatic event. I do not find that these difficulties would reasonably cause her to forget an international trip with her persecutors after they demanded she convert to Islam and submit her son to traditional rights.

subthemes.text:
[50] No claim was advanced on behalf of the American Minor Appellant against the US. The Principal Appellant confirmed in testimony that the Minor American Appellant has no fear of returning to the US.73 The RPD found that she is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.74 Counsel argues that the RPD's denial of the American Minor Appellant's claim is a "contravention of the principle of family unity."75 I disagree. Canadian jurisprudence is clear that the principle of family unity is not incorporated into the Convention refugee test at section 96 of the IRPA and the person in need of protection test at subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.76

[51] In support of her argument, Counsel relies on the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Handbook, which notes that the family is entitled to protection and emphasizes the importance of maintaining the unity of refugee families.77 However, the Handbook is also clear that "[t]he 1951 Convention does not incorporate the principle of family unity in the definition of the term refugee."78 Moreover, "family unity is not a concept that exists in Canadian refugee law."79 As the Federal Court found in Garcia Garcia, "the concept of family unity is not a valid argument because it 'does not relieve a claimant of the onus of demonstrating that he falls within the definition of 'Convention refugee'."80 The IRPA's family reunification objective is achieved by allowing protected persons in Canada to include their family members on their applications for permanent residence.81 Counsel also argues that the denial of the Minor American Appellant's claim results in "undue hardship."82 However, the RPD and the RAD do not have jurisdiction to consider humanitarian and compassionate factors.83

[52] Where a Claimant may return safely to one country of citizenship, the claim cannot succeed.84 Having not advanced claims against each of her countries of nationality, I find that the American Minor Appellant has not established her claim under sections 96 or 97(1) of the IRPA.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] These are my reasons for dismissing the appeals of XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Principal Appellant) and her children, XXXX XXXX XXXX (the American Minor Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Minor Appellant) and confirming the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) that they are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

[2] The Appellants are citizens of Nigeria. The American Minor Appellant is also a citizen of the United States (US). The Principal Appellant alleges that her in-laws will force her to become Muslim and that they will force the Minor Appellant and Minor American Appellant to undergo traditional rites, including incisions. She alleges that she has divorced her ex-husband, who remains in the US.

[3] The RPD denied the American Minor Appellant's claim as no claim was advanced on her behalf against the US. The RPD rejected the Appellants' claims based on material credibility concerns. In particular, the RPD found that the Principal Appellant lacked credibility based on inconsistencies and omissions related to multiple issues, including: (1) Her religion; (2) When she learned of her in-laws traditional rites; (3) Whether she was living in hiding in Nigeria or travelling in Saudi Arabia. She has provided new evidence, some of which I have admitted.

[4] Counsel argues that the RPD's credibility assessment is "not intelligible" and "derived from the Panel's scepticism rather than a reasoned assessment of the evidence."1 I disagree. I have independently assessed the Record and I find that the RPD decision is correct. While I have identified one error in the RPD's decision, I find that its overall determination is correct. The RPD correctly identified material inconsistencies in evidence which go to the heart of the claim. I further find that the RPD was correct to deny the American Minor Appellant's claim.
DECISION
[5] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
BACKGROUND

[6] The Principal Appellant alleges the following in her Basis of Claim (BOC) form:
* She is a "Converted Muslim (born Christian)"; and
* She comes "from a [M]uslim family but converted to Christianity while I was in secondary school, although my parents were not happy they accepted it."2

[7] She alleges that her family arranged for her to marry a Muslim man. She alleges that she continued to freely practice her Christian faith. After she married at the age of twenty-one, she gave birth to a son, the Minor Appellant. Following the birth, she alleges that her husband's family insisted that she begin practising Islam and that her son bear the family's facial incisions. After her son turned one, she alleges that she was informed the incisions would soon be performed. She objected and went into hiding in XXXX 2014 with her husband's help. She alleges that she remained in hiding in Nigeria until her husband secured US visas for the family.

[8] The Appellants arrived in the US in XXXX 2015. The American Minor Appellant was born in XXXX 2015. The Principal Appellant divorced her husband in XXXX 2016. She began a new relationship in the US and became pregnant. This relationship broke down. In XXXX 2018, the Appellants travelled irregularly to Canada to initiate their refugee claims. The Principal Appellant's third child was born in Canada in XXXX 2018 and is a Canadian citizen. In a XXXX 2020 BOC amendment, the Principal Appellant alleges that her in-laws continue searching for her in Nigeria.3

[10] The Appellants' claims were rejected on XXXX XXXX, 2020. They provide the following proposed new evidence on appeal:
a. A psychotherapy report, dated XXXX XXXX, 2020; and
b. An affidavit from the Principal Appellant's mother dated XXXX XXXX, 2020.4

[11] According to subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA),5 I can only accept evidence that:
i. Arose after the RPD decision; or
ii. Was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or
iii. Could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances before the decision.

[12] If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.6 According to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA,7 I may only hold an oral hearing where the accepted new evidence:
i. Raises a serious issue with respect to the Appellant's credibility; and
ii. Is central to the decision of the claim; and
iii. If accepted, justifies allowing or rejecting the claim.

[13] I find that the evidence in item (a) is admissible but does not require a hearing. I find that the evidence in item (b) is inadmissible.
The evidence in item (a) is admissible but does not require a hearing

[14] The psychotherapy report in item (a) is dated August 13, 2020. The report indicates that the Principal Appellant "is exhibiting symptoms consistent with post-traumatic stress, generalized anxiety, and major depression."8 Counsel argues that the Appellant was only aware of her psychological difficulties after the RPD rejection. On this basis, I find the report is admissible under 110(4). It is credible for the purposes of admission as it is issued by a psychotherapist. Counsel argues that "[t]he Psych report shows that the Appellant was pregnant during the hearing."9 I disagree. The psychotherapy report does not mention any pregnancy during the hearing. It states that the Principal Appellant was pregnant when she entered Canada.10 The report provides information that was not before the RPD and it is relevant to an assessment of the Principal Appellant's credibility. I admit item (a) into evidence. I find that it does not require a hearing under 110(6) as it does not justify allowing or rejecting the claim.11
The affidavit evidence in item (b) is inadmissible and cannot trigger a hearing under 110(6)

[15] The affidavit in item (b) was purportedly sworn by the Principal Appellant's mother on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020. It includes an allegation that in XXXX 2020, her home was visited by the Appellants' persecutors demanding to know their location and threatening that the next visit will be deadly.12 I find that the evidence post-dates the RPD's negative determination and therefore meets the requirements of subsection 110(4). However, I do not find the evidence to be credible having regard to the source and circumstances in which it came into existence.
There are credibility concerns with the evidence in item (b) which makes it inadmissible

[16] Counsel argues that the new evidence is credible because it is a "sworn statement of facts" before a Nigerian Notary Public.13 However, the Principal Appellant's mother has not signed above the line 'deponent.'14 This despite the fact that the document bears the stamp, seal and signature of a notary public indicating that the document was sworn on XXXX XXXX, 2020.15 Nothing in evidence or in Counsel's submissions comments on this irregularity.

[17] There is a rebuttable presumption that documents issued by foreign authorities are genuine.16 However, I find that there are irregularities on the face of the evidence which undermines its credibility and reliability and rebuts this presumption. The objective evidence states that "an affidavit will carry 'the signature of the deponent, the signature of the Commissioner for Oaths/Notary that swore the document, and the seal/stamp of the court/Notary.'"17 The Nigerian Evidence Act at section 117(4) requires that "an affidavit when sworn shall be signed by the deponent or if he cannot write or is blind, marked by him personally with his mark."18 Where the declarant was prevented from placing a signature on the statement, the Nigerian Evidence Act at section 119(3) requires a 'mark' be applied and that "the jurat shall state that fact, and that the mark was made in the presence of the person before whom it was taken."19 No such reference is made in the jurat of the declaration before me.20

[18] I acknowledge that superficial errors should not be unreasonably focused on in assessing a document's credibility as "clerical errors are possible even in countries where public administration have access to vast resources."21 However, I do not find these irregularities to be mere clerical errors. The signature, stamp and seal of a notary public are security features added to a sworn statement. They confirm that the deponent or affiant has appeared before the commissioner or notary and has sworn or affirmed as to the contents of the statement. It is only after this happens that a document is signed, stamped, and sealed by the notary or commissioner. It simply is not credible that a notary public would stamp and sign an affidavit without it first being signed by the deponent. The Federal Court found in Morka that the RPD's rejection of an unsigned affidavit was reasonable, noting that such an anomaly is apparent on its face.22 I find that these irregularities undermine the credibility of the source and circumstances in which the affidavit came into existence. The RAD is entitled to assess a document's irregularities in evaluating its credibility under the Singh factors.23

[19] I have also taken into consideration the stamps and seal present on the document. However, I do not find that this resolves the credibility concerns as it does not explain why the Principal Appellant's mother did not sign the affidavit or why a notary public signed the document in the absence of the signature of deponent.

[20] I also have concerns with the content of the statement. The Principal Appellant's mother alleges that she is Christian and the Principal Appellant "grew up in a Christian home."24 This differs from the Principal Appellant's own inconsistent evidence about her religious upbringing, including that she comes from a Muslim family and converted to Christianity against her parents' wishes.25 Nothing in evidence or submissions comments on the inconsistency as between the Principal Appellant's evidence and her mother's statement.

[21] As I have credibility concerns regarding the source and circumstances in which the evidence in item (b) came into existence, I do not find it credible. I therefore find it inadmissible.
The evidence in item (b) is inadmissible and cannot trigger a hearing under 110(6)

[22] Credibility is a consideration when: (1) assessing the admissibility of new evidence; and (2) assessing whether there is jurisdiction to convene a hearing. These two determinations are separate assessments that should not be conflated.26 First, all potential new evidence must meet the criteria in 110(4) and Singh, which includes a credibility assessment. The RAD can only accept new evidence that is credible.27 Second, if the new evidence is credible for admission, in consideration of its source and the circumstances in which it came into existence, it then will be assessed to see if it meets the criteria for an oral hearing. A document that is lacking in credibility, even if it is related to an Appellant's credibility, does not trigger an oral hearing under 110(6). The point of a RAD hearing is not to determine whether the new evidence is credible for admission, but rather to evaluate whether otherwise credible new evidence raises a serious credibility issue and justifies a reassessment of the overall credibility of the claim.28
[23] In this case, the evidence described in item (b) is not credible and therefore is not admissible. It does not satisfy 110(6) and I do not have jurisdiction to hold an oral hearing.
ANALYSIS

[24] The RAD's role is to decide if the RPD made the correct decision.29 I have independently assessed the evidence to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellants, the RPD erred. The Appellants are responsible for raising any grounds of appeal that arise from the RPD decision.30

[25] The Appellants argue that the RPD erred, as follows:
* In exhibiting "clear bias";
* In microscopically assessing the evidence and failing to accept that the Principal Appellant's pregnancy reasonably explains her error in describing her religion, and her failure to mention her trip to Saudi Arabia and XXXX, and other BOC omissions; and
* In contravening the principle of family unity.

[26] In assessing whether there are valid reasons to doubt the Appellants' credibility, I have considered the Principal Appellant's post-secondary education.31 I also note that she completed her BOC and amendment with the benefit of Counsel in English. I have also considered the Principal Appellants' psychotherapy report, which indicates that she "is exhibiting symptoms consistent with post-traumatic stress, generalized anxiety, and major depression."32 The psychotherapist indicates that the Principal Appellant self-reports "problems with concentration and focus which interferes with fluidity of thought and daily tasks" and "impaired short-term recall (i.e. short term memory loss)."33 I accept that the Principal Appellant is exhibiting these symptoms. Counsel argues that the Principal Appellant's pregnancy and psychological symptoms explain the inconsistencies in evidence. I disagree, as set out below.

[27] The RPD applied the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution (the Gender Guideline).34 Counsel has not identified any error in the RPD's use of the Gender Guideline, and I find none in my independent assessment. I am mindful that women refugee Claimants may face special problems in demonstrating that their claims are credible. However, I do not find that the Gender Guideline reasonably explains the material inconsistencies and omissions in evidence. The credibility concerns do not relate to a difficulty in providing evidence about gender-based harm or other traumatic events.

[28] After independently assessing all the evidence, I find that the RPD did err in one of its findings but that its overall determination is correct. I find that material credibility concerns were not reasonably explained, and that the presumption of truthfulness is rebutted.
The RPD did not display a reasonable apprehension of bias
[29] Counsel argues that the RPD exhibited "clear bias."35 I find that this argument is without merit. The RPD did not display a reasonable apprehension of bias.

[30] In Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board, the Supreme Court of Canada set out the test to determine the existence of a reasonable apprehension of bias:
[The] test is "what would an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically - and having thought the matter through - conclude. Would he think that it is more likely than not that [the decision-maker], whether consciously or unconsciously, would not decide fairly."36

[31] The grounds for the apprehension of bias must be substantial, and a high burden rests on the Appellant who seeks to establish either an actual bias or an apprehension of bias.37 A real likelihood of bias must be demonstrated.38 An allegation cannot rest on "mere suspicion, pure conjecture or mere impressions" and it "must be supported by material evidence."39 Counsel has failed to provide any examples which would support a finding that a reasonable person would conclude that the RPD would not decide fairly. Counsel merely disagrees with the RPD's findings. I find that an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically, would not think it more likely than not that the RPD would not decide fairly. Having independently assessed the entire Record, including the audio-recording, I find that the RPD did not display a reasonable apprehension of bias. As discussed below, the RPD was correct to draw negative credibility inferences based on significant inconsistencies in the evidence.
The RPD's overall credibility assessment is correct
Testimony about two demands for son's facial incision is not inconsistent

[32] The RPD found that the Principal Appellant provided inconsistent evidence about when she learned about the incision rites and that she omitted a family meeting from the BOC. Having independently assessed the evidence, I find no inconsistency or omission arises. In her BOC, the Principal Appellant describes learning about the facial incisions after the birth of her son and she also describes an incident after her son turned one year old where she was informed that the incision rites would soon be completed. This is consistent with her testimony.40 In addition, while she did not explicitly identify the incident after her son turned one year old as a "family meeting", she was clear in her BOC that she was "informed by the family."41 I find that the RPD erred and I do not rely on this RPD finding in my independent assessment.
Material inconsistency about religion

[33] In her BOC, the Principal Appellant provided inconsistent accounts of her religion. She states that she is a "Converted Muslim (born Christian)" and also that she comes "from a [M]uslim family but converted to Christianity while I was in secondary school, although my parents were not happy they accepted it."42 She testified that she is Christian and converted to Christianity in high school.43 She also testified that her father is Muslim and her Mother is Christian.44 When asked to explain the inconsistency in evidence, she explained that she made a mistake, she was pregnant when she came Canada, and she meant to be consistent in her BOC that she converted to Christianity.45 The RPD did not accept this explanation, finding it reasonable for her to be consistent about her religion and religious conversion throughout her BOC and testimony.46 The RPD further found that this is material to the claim as she alleged that her in-laws wanted to force her to convert to Islam and accept the family traditions.47 I agree.

[34] I find that the Principal Appellant's pregnancy and psychological symptoms do not reasonably explain her inconsistent statements about her own religion. I appreciate that pregnancy can cause forgetfulness and that the Principal Appellant struggles with short term-recall and her concentration difficulties interfere with her fluidity of thought. However, I do not find that these difficulties reasonably explain her inconsistent statements about her own religion. Her religion and religious upbringing are straightforward matters that do not relate to a recent or traumatic event. It has not been established that a difficulty with concentration would cause her to incorrectly state that she was born Christian and converted to Islam. The inconsistency about whether she was born Christian and converted to Islam, or was instead born in a Muslim family and converted to Christianity against her parent's wishes, is material. It is because of her Christian religion that she alleges that her in-laws want to force her to convert to Islam.

[35] Counsel argues that the inconsistency arises from an "obvious mistake while filling the BOC form."48 I disagree. The Principal Appellant wrote that she is a "Converted Muslim (born Christian)" in her own BOC.49 This is not an obvious mistake or minor typographical error. At the beginning of the RPD hearing, she confirmed that she completed and read her BOC in English and that it is complete, true, and correct.50 I accept that the high-stakes context of the RPD hearing can exacerbate a Claimant's inability to retrieve specific details of the past. However, this does not reasonably explain the Principal Appellant's inability to consistently recall what religion she was raised in and currently practices when completing her BOC in English with Counsel. She also filed an amendment with Counsel which offered no correction.51

[36] I also disagree with Counsel's argument that the inconsistency is microscopic.52 It is the Principal Appellant's Christian faith which grounds her claim. It is because she is Christian that she alleges that her in-laws have demanded she convert to Islam. This is not a peripheral detail. Her religion forms the underlying reason for her fear and is material to the claim. Moreover, her allegation that she comes from a Muslim family and her parents disapproved of her conversion to Christianity conflicts with her testimony that her mother is Christian.

[37] In her submissions, Counsel relies on Kanapathipillai and Attakora.53 However, these decisions are distinguishable and do not assist the Appellants. The erroneous credibility finding in Kanapathipillai was based on a POE statement made without Counsel and while using an interpreter. The erroneous credibility finding in Attakora was based on the plausibility of the Applicant's escape through a small hole and whether he had established a knee injury absent medical evidence. In contrast, the credibility concerns in the Appellants' case arise from inconsistencies and omissions in their own BOC narrative, drafted in English with the assistance of Counsel. In my view, these credibility concerns are neither microscopic nor overzealous.

[38] I agree with the RPD that it is reasonable to expect the Principal Appellant to provide consistent evidence about her faith and her religious upbringing. The RPD correctly drew a negative inference. I find that the inconsistency is material and undermines the Appellants' credibility.
Material omission of trip to Saudi Arabia while allegedly living in hiding in Nigeria

[39] In her BOC, the Principal Appellant alleges that she fled into hiding in Nigeria shortly after her son's first birthday.54 She alleges that she remained in hiding in Nigeria from XXXX 2014 until she fled to the US in XXXX 2015.55 She testified that in XXXX and XXXX 2015 she was fleeing between various cities in Nigeria.56 However, her own passport indicates that she was not in Nigeria throughout XXXX 2015 but was in fact on an Omra (Umrah) visa in Saudi Arabia.57 When confronted with her Saudi Arabia trip at the RPD hearing, she explained that she "didn't recall that event" when completing her BOC as she was pregnant and "it's been a long time."58 The RPD did not accept this explanation, finding that it does not reasonably explain her evidence that she was in two places at once.59 I agree.

[40] Counsel argues that the RPD failed to consider the Principal Appellant's explanation for the trip to Saudi Arabia.60 I disagree. The RPD's concern was not with her decision to take this trip, but rather with the omission of the trip from the BOC and her allegation that she was in hiding in Nigeria when she was in fact travelling in Saudi Arabia. The trip to Saudi Arabia in XXXX 2015 undermines her alleged time in hiding in Nigeria.

[41] The Principal Appellant completed her BOC in English and filed an amendment where she failed to correct her allegation that she was hiding in Nigeria during this trip abroad.61 I do not find that her failure to recall this event is explained by her pregnancy or psychological symptoms. The Saudi Arabia trip is not connected to a short-term memory or a traumatic event. I appreciate that pregnancy can cause forgetfulness and that the Principal Appellant has trouble with short term-recall and her concentration difficulties interfere with her fluidity of thought. However, I do not find that these difficulties would reasonably cause her to state that she was in hiding in Nigeria when she was in fact travelling abroad, in Saudi Arabia. Whether the Principal Appellant was in hiding in Nigeria in XXXX 2015, as alleged, is material to her claim. This is not a peripheral detail. Her Saudi Arabia trip undermines her allegation that she was living in hiding from her persecutors in Nigeria during this period.

[42] I agree with the RPD that it is reasonable to expect the Principal Appellant to include her trip to Saudi Arabia in her BOC and provide consistent evidence about whether she was hiding in Nigeria or travelling abroad. The RPD correctly drew a negative inference. In my independent assessment, I find the BOC omission and inconsistency undermine the Appellants' credibility.
Material omission of trip to XXXX from the BOC

[43] The Principal Appellant also failed to disclose a further trip in her BOC, this time to XXXX in XXXX 2014 with the in-laws that she fears. The Principal Appellant explained that "we were in XXXX before those, they started threatening me" and that before this trip there was "nothing serious about it."62 However, this conflicts with her BOC where she alleges that the threats began shortly after her son's birth in XXXX 2013, when the "harassment increased" and she was "severally [sic] mistreated by my mother-in-law."63 The Principal Appellant also explained that she omitted the XXXX trip because she was pregnant and forgetful when she wrote her BOC.64 The RPD found that the omission was not reasonably explained.65 I agree.

[44] Counsel raises one error with respect to this RPD finding - that the RPD improperly drew a negative inference from the fact that the in-laws never tried to harm the Minor Appellant on this trip.66 In my view, Counsel has misapprehended the RPD's finding. The RPD did not draw an adverse inference because the persecutors did not harm the Minor Appellant. While the RPD expressed "surprise" that the Minor Appellant was not harmed on this trip, it drew an adverse inference based on the omission of this trip from the BOC.67 In my independent assessment, I draw no adverse inference based on the absence of harm on this trip. I agree with the RPD that the trip to XXXX is material to the claim. It was taken with the agents of persecution after the Principal Appellant alleges in her BOC that the harm, harassment, and mistreatment increased.

[45] In my independent assessment, I have considered whether the Principal Appellant's pregnancy and psychological evidence reasonably explain the BOC omission. I appreciate that pregnancy can cause forgetfulness and that the Principal Appellant has trouble with short term-recall and her concentration difficulties interfere with her fluidity of thought. However, the XXXX trip is not connected to a short-term memory or a traumatic event. I do not find that these difficulties would reasonably cause her to forget an international trip with her persecutors after they demanded she convert to Islam and submit her son to traditional rights.

[46] The RPD correctly drew a negative inference. In my independent assessment, I find the BOC omission, and inconsistent explanations, undermine the Appellants' credibility.
Counsel's argument about the totality of the evidence lacks substance and specificity

[47] Counsel also references Federal Court jurisprudence that holds that the totality of the evidence must be considered before reaching a decision.68 I agree. However, Counsel fails to identify what, if any, evidence was not considered by the RPD. Counsel fails to advance any substantive or specific argument in this regard, as required by RAD Rule 3(3)(g)(ii).69 It is not the RAD's role to come up with ideas to assist the Appellants in succeeding with an appeal.70

[48] I have considered the totality of the evidence. In my independent assessment, I note that the Appellants provided supporting affidavits and a church letter. This evidence indicates that the Principal Appellant "grew up in a Christian home" or "was from a Christian home" and that her mother is a Christian church member.71 This differs from the Principal Appellant's own inconsistent evidence about her religious upbringing, including that she comes from a Muslim family and converted to Christianity against her parents' wishes.72 Without determining whether these apparent discrepancies between the Appellants' evidence and their supporting documents should lead to an adverse credibility inference, I simply note for present purposes that increased scrutiny of the supporting evidence by the RPD would not necessarily have assisted the Appellants. Given the inconsistencies for which there is no reasonable explanation, the central allegation of harm from the in-laws is not credible.
Credibility summary

[49] After independently assessing the complete Record, I find that the Appellants are, on a balance of probabilities, not credible. I find that they have not credibly established, on a balance of probabilities, that they are being pursued by their agents of harm to enforce a religious conversion or the forced imposition of traditional rites. They have not credibly established that they face a serious possibility of persecution or subsection 97(1) risk upon return to Nigeria.
The principle of family unity is not incorporated into sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA

[50] No claim was advanced on behalf of the American Minor Appellant against the US. The Principal Appellant confirmed in testimony that the Minor American Appellant has no fear of returning to the US.73 The RPD found that she is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.74 Counsel argues that the RPD's denial of the American Minor Appellant's claim is a "contravention of the principle of family unity."75 I disagree. Canadian jurisprudence is clear that the principle of family unity is not incorporated into the Convention refugee test at section 96 of the IRPA and the person in need of protection test at subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.76

[51] In support of her argument, Counsel relies on the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Handbook, which notes that the family is entitled to protection and emphasizes the importance of maintaining the unity of refugee families.77 However, the Handbook is also clear that "[t]he 1951 Convention does not incorporate the principle of family unity in the definition of the term refugee."78 Moreover, "family unity is not a concept that exists in Canadian refugee law."79 As the Federal Court found in Garcia Garcia, "the concept of family unity is not a valid argument because it 'does not relieve a claimant of the onus of demonstrating that he falls within the definition of 'Convention refugee'."80 The IRPA's family reunification objective is achieved by allowing protected persons in Canada to include their family members on their applications for permanent residence.81 Counsel also argues that the denial of the Minor American Appellant's claim results in "undue hardship."82 However, the RPD and the RAD do not have jurisdiction to consider humanitarian and compassionate factors.83

[52] Where a Claimant may return safely to one country of citizenship, the claim cannot succeed.84 Having not advanced claims against each of her countries of nationality, I find that the American Minor Appellant has not established her claim under sections 96 or 97(1) of the IRPA.
CONCLUSION

[53] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
